# What is Git?

## What is Git?

- Git is a free and open-source distributed version control system (VCS) designed
to track changes in source code and other files.

- Primarily, Git is a command line utility that runs locally on your machine.
  - Meaning, we will be using the command line.

- Git is **the** essential version control tool that provides both the foundation
	and safety net you need to take your projects to the next level of
	professionalism.
  - Or a tool to help you complete your homework.

## Why Git?

- According to the 2022 Stack Overflow developer survey, 96% of professional 
developers use Git.

- Git was built to work on the Linux kernel, meaning that it was built to
handle repositories with tens of millions of lines of code.

- As of 2025, the current version of the Linux kernel's source code is 1.7 GB.
Git stores the full history of the Linux project (1.4 million commits) in only
5.5 GB.

## What is version control and why do we need Git? {.smaller}

- Much like save states in a video game, Git allows us to save our projects
  progress when we choose.

- Gives you security in knowing that if something goes wrong you can always go
	back.
  - Allows you to take risks in your project that you normally would not.

- Keeps your progress organized, visible and sequential.

- Provides a multitude of quality of life features.
  - Writing code or finishing a project is hard enough as is. You should not
	have to worry about little things going wrong.


## What is GitHub?

- GitHub is company owned by Microsoft, they will host your project on their
servers and allow you view them through their website.

- GitHub uses Git as their backbone, but they provide a lot of extra
functionality.
	- Especially for working collaboratively.

- GitHub is the platform of choice for almost all open source software. But also
closed source software.
  - Meaning if you aim to work on software you will likely be using GitHub.


## Why GitHub? {.smaller}

- Since your project will be uploaded to the cloud, you can work on projects
across your devices.
  - No excuses that your laptop broke.

- There are other websites that will host your projects on their server: ie.
GitLab, Bitbucket.
  - Although, GitHub is the most popular.

**Build and share your portfolio**.

- GitHub is like a social media for your code.

- People can naturally find your projects.
	- Or you could share them easily.

- You can search through millions of open source projects and even contribute to
them.

- **Makes collaboration simple**.


# Setup & Installation {.smaller}

## GitHub {.smaller}

If you have not already, you should create an account on GitHub:

1) Visit the GitHub website: [GitHub signup](https://github.com/signup). Enter
your credentials, email and password.

2) **Enable 2FA**

> As of March 2023, GitHub required all users who contribute code on GitHub.com
> to enable one or more forms of two-factor authentication (2FA).

You can configure two-factor authentication (2FA) using a TOTP app on mobile or
desktop or via text message.

## Installing Git {.smaller}

Git runs locally on your system. Meaning the process of installing Git is
different per operating system. We will operate Git using the command line.

## macOS {.smaller}

There are a few ways to install Git on your Mac, but the easiest is to use
Homebrew, a package manager that allows you to easily install other
applications.

**Install Homebrew**

1. Visit [brew.sh](https://brew.sh) in your browser. You will find the following
command:

``` 
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
```
2. Copy and paste this command into your terminal. Hit enter to run it.

**Use Homebrew to install Git**

3. Once Homebrew has finished installing, run this command:

```
brew install git
```

4. Once installation is complete, verify Git is installed:

```
git --version
```

## Windows {.smaller} 

The most simple to install Git on Windows is to use the official Git installer:
 
1. Visit the official [Git website](https://git-scm.com/install/windows)
 
2. Download the "Standalone Installer." If you're on a 64-bit system, choose "Git
for Windows/x64 Setup."
 
3. After the download finishes, find the file (Downloads folder) and follow the
installation instructions.
 
4. Now search for "Git Bash" in your Start menu. If it appears, you have
successfully installed Git on your Windows device.

## Set up SSH {.smaller}

1. In your terminal, or GitBash run the following:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
```
- When prompted for a file location, press Enter to accept the default.
- Optionally set a passphrase for extra security.

2. Run the following:

```bash
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```
3. **Copy the entire output.**

4. Go to GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys

5. Click New SSH key

6. Give it a title (e.g., "My Laptop")

7. Paste your public key

8. Click Add SSH key

## Initial configuration

:::{style="margin-top: 15%;"}
```bash
git config --add --global user.name "github_username_here"

git config --add --global user.email "email@something.com"

git config --add --global init.defaultBranch main
```
:::

# Git Fundamentals

## What is a Repository?

- A repository (or "repo") is the directory in which all of the data of your
project is kept.

- A Git repository will always have a `.git/` subdirectory.
  - This is how Git tracks everything: your commits, branches, and history
   	are all stored here.

::: {.callout-warning}
### Never manually edit the `.git/` directory
Modifying or deleting anything inside `.git/` can corrupt your repository.
:::

## Creating Your First Repository {.smaller}
::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

1. Create a new repository on GitHub.
    - Give it a name and leave all other settings as default for now.

2. Copy the SSH link from the **"Code"** dropdown on your new repository's
page.

3. Now, open your terminal and **change directories** to where you would like your
	 project to stay:

```bash
cd ~/Documents
```

4. Clone the repository:

```bash
git clone [paste your ssh link here]
```

> This will create a new directory with the name of your repository, initialize
> a Git repo inside it, and connect it to GitHub automatically.

5. `cd` into your new repository:

```bash
cd [repository-name]
```

6. Run:

```bash
git init
```
:::

## What is a Commit? {.smaller}

- The core functionality of Git is the ability to save your work.
  - Git packages these saves as **commits**.

- A commit is a permanent snapshot of your project's files at a specific point
in time

- Commits act as a "save point" in your project's history.

- Commits are ordered and structured, each subsequent save (commit) points to
the previous commit.


## How do we control which files get Committed {.smaller} 

- Before we make a commit, we have to tell Git what files we would like to save.

- Git labels every file in your repository with one of three states:
  - These states are how we control what gets committed and what does not.

| State       | Description                                     |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `untracked` | Git is not tracking this file at all.           |
| `modified`  | A tracked file that has changes not yet staged. |
| `staged`    | Marked for inclusion in the next commit.        |

- Once a file is staged, then we can commit it.

## Your First Commit {.smaller}
::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

Every repository needs a good "readme", it is the landing page of your
repository. You should precisely explain the purpose of your repository. You
should also provide any other additional information that someone interested in
your project may need.

1. Open the IDE or text editor of your choice.
  - Choose whatever program you typically use to do work.

2. Within your repository, create a new file called `README.md`.

3. Inside the file, give a description of your project, for example:

```text
This is an example Homework assignment.
```

4. **Save the file**.

5. Run the following:

```bash
git status
```
> You should see `README.md` listed as an **untracked** file.

:::

## Staging Your Changes {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
We have finished editing our file. Now we need to tell Git what to track.

1. Run the following:

```bash
git add README.md
```
> This marks the file for inclusion in the next commit.

2. Then check the repository status.

```bash
git status
```
> You should now see `README.md` listed under **"Changes to be committed"**. It
> is now in the **staged** state.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Staging all changes at once
You can stage all changed and untracked files at once with:
```bash
git add .
```
Be careful with this, make sure you are not accidentally staging files you
did not intend to commit.
:::
:::

## Making the Commit

Run the following:

```bash
git commit -m "Initial, added README"
```

- Every commit requires a **commit message**.
  - A short description of what changed and why.

- A good commit message is short but descriptive, e.g.
`"Initial added README"` rather than `"changes"`.

:::{.callout-tip}
### The 50/70 rule
50 is the maximum number of characters of the commit title, and 72 is the
maximum character length of the commit body
:::

## What happens when you make a commit? {.smaller}

- Git saves a snapshot of all staged files at that moment in time.
- Git generates a unique hash (e.g. `a3f8c2d...`) to identify the commit.
- Git records your name, email, and timestamp.
- Git updates the `.git/` directory.
- Finally the commit is added to your commit history.

You can use `git log` to check your commit history.

**What you should never commit**

- Large datasets (`.csv`, `.zip`, etc.)
- Rendered outputs or build artifacts
- Installed dependencies or libraries
- Environment or OS-specific files (`.DS_Store`, etc.)
- Anything copyrighted or sensitive (API keys, passwords)

## When should I commit my changes?

- A commit should represent a single "atomic" unit of work: one coherent feature,
bug fix, or refactoring
  - Avoid mixing unrelated changes, such as fixing a bug and refactoring code in
	the same commit.

- Treat local commits like a save point in a video game that you can always go
back to.
	- Ask yourself: "would I be comfortable losing the progress I have made since
	the previous commit?"

- Many developers commit every 15 to 60 minutes or whenever they finish a "full
thought".

## Uploading Changes to GitHub  {.smaller}

Now that we have saved our work locally we are ready to send the changes to our
GitHub repository. 

- GitHub hosts a bare Git repository for you, on their server.
  - So our GitHub repo is actually a entirely different repository on a
	different computer.

- Sending the changes from your local repo to an external one is called a `push`

Run this to upload your changes:
```bash
git push origin main
```

> This syncs your local commits to your GitHub repository. `origin` is the name
> of your remote connection to GitHub. `main` is the name of the branch you are
> pushing to.

After pushing, navigate to your repository on GitHub and reload the page.

## When should I push my changes?

- It is best practice to only push your changes to GitHub when you are confident
	that your local repository is in a good state.
	- You know that you will not need to undo changes and modify you commit
	history.

- There are some scenarios in which pushing will prevent you from altering your
	commit history in a standard way.

- You should treat you GitHub repository as the place where your stable work
	goes.

## The Git & GitHub Workflow {.smaller}
::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

Putting it all together, the basic workflow is:

1. Create or edit files in your repository.
2. Check the status of your repository.
```bash
git status
```
3. Stage the changes you want to commit.
```bash
git add <file>
```
4. Commit the staged changes with a descriptive message.
```bash
git commit -m "your message here"
```
5. Push your commits to GitHub.
```bash 
git push origin main
```
::: {.callout-tip}
### Get in the habit of running `git status` constantly
Before and after every command, run `git status`. It will always tell you
exactly what state your repository is in and help you avoid surprises.
:::
:::

1. Navigate to this presentations GitHub repository.
  - There is a link to it from the CSAS 2026 website.

2. Find the `git_homework.md` file, click on it, copy its contents.

3. Create a new file in your own repository `git_homework.md`

4. Open the new file, and paste in the copied text.

5. Now, `add`, `commit` and `push` the file.
 
# Additional Basic Functionality

## .gitignore {.smaller}

- A `.gitignore` file tells Git which files and directories it should not
track.

- This is useful for keeping sensitive data, large files, and generated
files out of your repository.

**Common things to ignore**

- API keys and passwords
- Large data files (`.csv`, `.zip`, etc.)
- System files (`.DS_Store` on macOS)
- Generated files (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`)

## Example `.gitignore` {.smaller}

```text
# Ignore all CSV files.
*.csv

# Ignore macOS system files.
.DS_Store

# Ignore Python cache.
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# Ignore virtual environment folder.
.venv/
```

Create a `.gitignore` by making a new file in the root of your repository
named `.gitignore` and adding the patterns you want to ignore.

## Log

This command will show you your commit history and its structure. It also
provides the commit hashes, which can be useful if you need to single out a
commit.

```bash
git log
```
- This unformatted version can get messy if you have a large commit history.

``` bash
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents
```
- This version will show you a neat representation of you commit history across
all branches.

## Checkout
In earlier versions of Git `checkout` had many uses. Although, in modern
versions of it is primarily just used to look at the contents of previous
commits.

```bash
git checkout <commit hash>
```

:::{.callout-note}
Be careful not to commit to your current branch when checked out on a commit
other than the tip.
:::

## Diff {.smaller}

This command allows you to see the differences between various combinations of
files across commits.

```bash
git diff
```
- Compares your working tree vs the index (staging area). It shows changes you
haven't staged yet. Although the file must be tracked. 

```bash
git diff --staged
```
- Compares your staged files with the latest commit.

```bash
git diff HEAD
```
- Compares your staged and unstaged changes to the most recent commit.

## Restore

This command is useful if you want to restore a file quickly.

```bash
git restore <file>
```
- This command allows you to restore a file from the previous commit.

```bash
git restore --staged <file>
```
- This will remove the file from the staging area.

```bash
git restore --source COMMITHASH <file>
```
- This will restore a file form the specified commit.

## Reset

These commands let you reset your entire repository back to a previous commit.

``` bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```
This command will move back the HEAD pointer, but keep the working directory the
same, and restages your files.

``` bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```
This command will completely reset your entire repository back to the specified
commit.


# Branching

## What is a Branch? {.smaller}

- A branch is an independent line of development within a repository.

- By default, your repository has one branch called **main**. This is the
"official" version of your project.

- When you create a branch, you are creating an independent copy of the
codebase that you can make changes to without affecting **main**.

- When you are satisfied with your changes, you can merge your branch back
into **main**.


## Why use branches?

- Allows you to work on a new feature or fix a bug without risking breaking
the working version of your project.

- Enables multiple people to work on different features simultaneously without
interfering with each other.

## Creating and Switching Branches {.smaller}

1. Create a new branch:

```bash
git branch feature-branch
```

2. Switch to the new branch:

```bash
git switch feature-branch
```

::: {.callout-tip}
You can create and switch with one line like this:
```bash
git switch -c feature-branch
```
:::

3. Check which branch you are currently on:

```bash
git branch
```

> The branch with the `*` next to it is the branch you are currently on.

## Working on a Branch {.smaller}

Once you are on your new branch, the workflow is exactly the same as before:

1. Create and edit files.
2. Stage the changes with `git add`.
3. Commit the changes with `git commit -m "commit message"`.


Any commits you make will only affect your current branch. Your **main**
branch will remain unchanged.

Push your branch to GitHub:

```bash
git push origin feature-branch
```
- GitHub will not know about your branch until you push to it.

**Try this**
Create a new file `contents.md`, add, commit and push it to this branch.

## Merging Branches {.smaller}

- Once you are satisfied with the changes on your branch, you can merge it
back into **main**.

- First, switch back to **main**:

```bash
git switch main
```

- Then merge your branch into **main**:

```bash
git merge feature-branch
```

## Merge Conflicts {.smaller}

- A merge conflict occurs when two branches have made changes to the same
part of the same file.

- Git will not know which version to keep, so it will ask you to resolve the
conflict manually.

- Git will mark the conflict in the file like this:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
This is the version on main.
=======
This is the version on feature-branch.
>>>>>>> feature-branch
```

- You must edit the file to keep the version you want, removing the conflict
markers, then stage and commit the resolved file.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Avoiding Merge Conflicts
The best way to avoid merge conflicts is to keep branches short-lived and
focused on a single feature or fix, and to regularly sync your branch with
main using `git pull`.
:::

## Deleting a Branch {.smaller}

Once your branch has been merged, you can safely delete it:

```bash
git branch -d feature-branch
```

To delete the branch on GitHub as well:

```bash
git push origin --delete feature-branch
```

- You can also directly delete the branch using GitHub.

# Collaboration with GitHub

## What is a Pull Request? {.smaller}

- A Pull Request (PR) is a feature of GitHub that allows you to propose
merging changes from one branch into another.

- Pull Requests are the standard way to contribute to a project on GitHub,
whether it is your own or someone else's.

- A Pull Request gives collaborators the opportunity to **review your changes**
before they are merged into **main**.

**Why use Pull Requests?**

- Keeps the **main** branch stable and working.

- Creates a record of why and how changes were made.

- Allows collaborators to leave comments and suggest improvements before
changes are merged.

- Even on solo projects, PRs are a good habit - they give you a chance to
review your own changes.

## Opening a Pull Request {.smaller}

1. Push your branch to GitHub if you have not already:

```bash
git push origin feature-branch
```

2. Navigate to your repository on GitHub.

3. GitHub will display a prompt at the top of the page:
*"feature-branch had recent pushes"* - click **"Compare & pull request"**.

4. Fill in the Pull Request form:
    - **Title** - a short description of what your changes do.
    - **Description** - explain what you changed and why.

5. Click **"Create pull request"**.

## Reviewing a Pull Request {.smaller}

- Once a Pull Request is open, collaborators can:
    - **View the changes** made in the PR under the "Files changed" tab.
    - **Leave comments** on specific lines of code.
    - **Approve** the changes or **request changes** before merging.

- On a solo project you will typically review your own PR before merging.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Writing a Good PR Description
A good PR description answers three questions:
- What did you change?
- Why did you make this change?
- Is there anything the reviewer should pay special attention to?
:::

## Merging a Pull Request {.smaller}

Once the PR has been reviewed and approved:

1. Click **"Merge pull request"** on the PR page on GitHub.

2. Click **"Confirm merge"**.

3. Optionally delete the branch on GitHub by clicking
**"Delete branch"**.

4. Sync your local **main** branch with the changes:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
```

Any time the upstream repository (GitHub repo) has been updated, you have to download
the changes. This is done using `git pull`.

 - Only pulls changes from your current branch.

## The Full Collaboration Workflow {.smaller}

Putting it all together:

1. Create a new branch for your feature or fix.
```bash
git switch -c feature-branch
```
2. Make changes, stage and commit them.
```bash
git add .
git commit -m "description of changes"
```
3. Push the branch to GitHub.
```bash
git push origin feature-branch
```
4. Open a Pull Request on GitHub.
5. Review and merge the Pull Request.
6. Sync your local main branch.
```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
```
